lesson.title: The Timing Shift Nobody Notices Until It Matters: Phase Response
lesson.summary: Phase response tracks how much a circuit delays or advances its output relative to its input at each frequency, sweeping smoothly from no shift to a full 90 degree shift for a simple RC filter.
lesson.body:
Phase Angle describes the timing offset between two sinusoids of the same frequency, and Frequency Response established that a circuit's transfer function changes with frequency. Phase Response combines these two ideas by tracking specifically how the phase angle of H(jw) changes as frequency sweeps from low to high, separate from what happens to the magnitude, which is covered on its own in the next section. A negative phase angle here means the output lags the input, arriving slightly later in time at that frequency, which is the physically meaningful interpretation behind every number that follows.

Return once more to the RC low pass filter with R = 1000 ohms and C = 1 microfarad, corner frequency wc = 1000 rad/s. For this filter, H(jw) = 1/(1+jwRC), and the phase angle of H is theta(w) = -arctan(wRC), the negative sign appearing because the denominator's phase gets subtracted when a complex number is in the denominator of a ratio.

Evaluate this at three frequencies to see the full sweep. At w = 100 rad/s, one decade below the corner, wRC = 0.1, so theta = -arctan(0.1) = -5.711 degrees, a barely noticeable shift. At w = 1000 rad/s, exactly the corner frequency, wRC = 1, so theta = -arctan(1) = -45.000 degrees exactly, the midpoint of the total possible phase swing. At w = 10000 rad/s, one decade above the corner, wRC = 10, so theta = -arctan(10) = -84.289 degrees, closing in on but not quite reaching -90 degrees.

These three numbers, -5.711, -45.000, and -84.289 degrees, trace out the characteristic shape of a first order low pass filter's phase response: nearly flat at 0 degrees far below the corner, sweeping rapidly through -45 degrees exactly at the corner, and flattening out again as it approaches but never quite reaches -90 degrees far above the corner. The theoretical limit of -90 degrees is only reached as w goes to infinity, since arctan(wRC) approaches 90 degrees but never equals it for any finite wRC.

Phase response matters just as much as magnitude response in real designs, because a phase shift is a time delay, and stacking multiple filter stages compounds those delays in ways that can distort a signal even when the magnitude response looks perfectly acceptable. Audio engineers worry about phase response when cascading filters so that different frequency components of a sound do not arrive at noticeably different times, and control engineers worry about it because excessive phase lag in a feedback loop is a leading cause of instability. A related, useful quantity is group delay, essentially how quickly the phase angle changes with frequency, which is largest right around the corner frequency where theta(w) swings from near 0 toward near -90 degrees most rapidly.

The exact -45 degree value at the corner frequency, verified above, is one of the most useful landmarks for identifying a first order filter's corner frequency directly from a measured phase plot.
